claim: Feeding the instruction diff back to the model produces a targeted fix and converges on a match.
evidence: Across 8 functions it rescued ZERO. Every match came on the first attempt. Best-of-N on the same budget got 6/8 vs 3/8. The model cannot invert 'this instruction differs' into 'this source change fixes it'; shown a diff it rewrites plausible-but-different C rather than converging.

claim: Independent best-of-N sampling beats sequential refinement at equal budget, because the answer is already in the model's distribution.
evidence: 6/8 vs 3/8 exact at identical budget. Direct proof of the mechanism: the same function resampled from an identical prompt scored 87.61%, 82.42%, then 100%.

claim: decomp-permuter can close a near-miss below 95%.
evidence: The permuter moves register allocation and never touches types or control flow. unlockRelocatableHeapBlock sat at 99.167% purely because the model declared an 18-byte struct against a real 20-byte one; 300s of permuting moved it nowhere. Confirmed by the repo's own skill docs.

claim: Struct size can be read arithmetically out of the target's index arithmetic and handed to the model as fact.
evidence: `sll 2; addu; sll 2` is unambiguously x20. That function went from stuck-at-99.167% (permuter could not help) to EXACT on the first draw once the stride was stated. *** RETRACTED: THIS HINT NEVER REACHED A PROMPT. *** The line composing stride/narrow-param/frame hints into hints_for_asm never applied -- the string replace did not match and the patch script printed 'patched' unconditionally. grep found zero references to the hint functions. So the evidence cited for this entry cannot have come from this hint; whatever moved those numbers, it was something else (sampling variance, KB context, or the pipeline). Downgraded to UNTESTED. Now wired in and asserted by tests/test_units.py::test_hints_mention_frame_and_stride.

claim: A dead `sw $aN, K($sp)` plus `andi 0xffff` at entry proves parameter N is 16-bit.
evidence: setRaceCameraMode(u16,u16) shows the pattern twice; the s32 control getRaceItemEffectType shows neither instruction. Detector verified on both, plus a deliberate conservative miss on spawnPatrolCourseObject. Shipped in the same bundled run; not isolated. *** RETRACTED: THIS HINT NEVER REACHED A PROMPT. *** The line composing stride/narrow-param/frame hints into hints_for_asm never applied -- the string replace did not match and the patch script printed 'patched' unconditionally. grep found zero references to the hint functions. So the evidence cited for this entry cannot have come from this hint; whatever moved those numbers, it was something else (sampling variance, KB context, or the pipeline). Downgraded to UNTESTED. Now wired in and asserted by tests/test_units.py::test_hints_mention_frame_and_stride.

claim: Statement line placement or blank lines change codegen.
evidence: The reference repo ran the control: this project builds without -g, so inserting blank lines anywhere yields a byte-identical object. Guidance suggesting otherwise assumes a debug-bearing build. IMPORTANT DISTINCTION: this refutes BLANK LINES, not LOGICAL statement line numbers. Workbench levers 23/25/33 state that uopt/ugen honor statement line boundaries even at -g0, and that cfe numbers statements by LOGICAL line -- so splicing two statements onto ONE physical line makes them tie on lineno and lets ready-list position decide the schedule. That is a different lever and is NOT refuted. Do not conflate them.

claim: Feeding the workspace's generated ctx.c gives useful type context.
evidence: ctx.c contains the preprocessed translation unit INCLUDING the target function's own body -- line 2326 was literally the answer to getRaceItemEffectType. Using it fabricates a 100% and invalidates every downstream number. Harmless upstream where the function is genuinely undone; fatal for evaluation.

claim: `sll 24` followed by `srl 24` is a u8 cast; with `sra 24` it is an s8 cast -- so the variable should be declared 8-bit.
evidence: Probably true but negligible surface area: only 15 shifts of 0x18 exist in the whole binary versus 2,970 of 0x10. A real s8 pair exists at 0x8007dd48 (sll 0x18 / sra 0x18), but a detector would fire on ~1 function in 2,113. Not worth prompt budget. Prevalence-check before implementing.
tested_on: frequency scan of the full SBK1 binary

claim: `void f(void)` uses 4 more bytes of stack than `void f()`.
evidence: Folded into a broader frame-size hint rather than tested alone. The general lever -- state the target frame size as a fact and list what moves it -- covers 1,874 of 2,113 functions, versus this single 4-byte case.

claim: `x > y` is emitted as `x >= y + 1` when y is a constant.
`&a[i]` inside a loop makes IDO keep an extra loop counter; `a + i` uses multiplication instead.
IDO unrolls small loops by 2 or 4; `continue;` or `i++; i--;` suppresses it.
Stating the target stack frame size as a fact, plus the levers that move it, prevents the whole-function offset noise a wrong frame causes.
evidence: Implemented; extraction verified (spawnPatrolCourseObject=24, frameless leaves=None). Prevalence checked first: 1,874 functions allocate a frame vs 15 byte-casts. Permuter README confirms --stack-diffs is weak, so a frame mismatch cannot be permuted away and must be fixed in source. Shipped in a run bundling three changes (context fix, narrow-param hint, frame hint): 7/41 -> 10/41 exact, mean 55.33 -> 69.26. Cannot be attributed alone; the large-tier recovery is mechanistically the context fix. *** RETRACTED: THIS HINT NEVER REACHED A PROMPT. *** The line composing stride/narrow-param/frame hints into hints_for_asm never applied -- the string replace did not match and the patch script printed 'patched' unconditionally. grep found zero references to the hint functions. So the evidence cited for this entry cannot have come from this hint; whatever moved those numbers, it was something else (sampling variance, KB context, or the pipeline). Downgraded to UNTESTED. Now wired in and asserted by tests/test_units.py::test_hints_mention_frame_and_stride.
tested_on: 41-function dev set, bundled with 2 other changes

claim: num_ctx=8192 is adequate for this task.
evidence: Context is shared by prompt, reasoning trace and answer. On large functions the model was truncated mid-statement and scored 0. updateCourseSelectCourseDescription's best attempt ends at 'if (widget->field1c >=' and one attempt was 40 bytes. This made ADDING context actively harmful on exactly the functions it should help most: large-tier mean fell 8.2% -> 0.1% under the pipeline while small rose 75.9->85.4 and medium 36.2->48.7. Fixed by sizing num_ctx from prompt length up to 32768. CONFIRMED BY FIX: after sizing num_ctx from prompt length, large-tier mean recovered 0.1% -> 33.3% and compile failures across the set fell 10 -> 4.
tested_on: 41-function dev set, per-tier breakdown + direct inspection

claim: A value-position `a && b` must be spelled the way cfe expands it -- `v = (a); if (v) { v = (b); }` -- which is byte-identical to the operator, while `v = 0; if (a && b) v = 1;`, if/else and branch-free forms cost hundreds of rows.
evidence: Compiler-general (not tagged IDO 7.1). Cheap as a prompt rule; detectability unclear. Check prevalence of value-position && before implementing.

claim: Folding two statements onto one physical line ties their lineno so ready-list position decides scheduling; as1's scheduler reads source line numbers.
evidence: Distinct from the refuted blank-line hypothesis. Applies to schedule-mismatch verdicts specifically, so it belongs behind the verdict router rather than in the first prompt.

claim: When registers and opcodes are exact but the frame is not, compare observed save-slot bytes against non-save frame bytes and work only the component that differs.
evidence: Pairs with the frame-size hint already shipped. Applies to frame-layout-mismatch verdicts.

claim: Workbench levers 34-39 apply to our target.
evidence: Levers 34-39 are explicitly prefixed 'IDO 7.1:'. SBK1 builds with IDO 5.3 (tools/ido-recomp/linux/cc, -O2 -mips1). Do not spend iterations on peep_reg, dispatch-parity or selector-temp levers -- they describe a different compiler version.

claim: Classifying the mismatch with n64-decomp-workbench and feeding that verdict's playbook levers beats routing on score alone.
source: n64-decomp-workbench; named in the SBK author's own writeup
evidence: DOWNGRADED from CONFIRMED on external review, and the downgrade is correct. The claim rested on exact 10 -> 12 while mean score FELL 69.26 -> 64.07; a 95% interval on that mean delta is roughly -10.42 to +0.04, i.e. inconclusive. It was also invalidated by a LATER finding in this same bank -- tier-means-underpowered-at-n10 showed an UNCHANGED tier moving +9.8 points, so a 2-function exact delta is inside noise. The mechanism remains sound (score cannot distinguish a relocation error from a register-allocation one) and the routing is KEPT, but it is not measured. Needs repeated paired runs with fixed seeds.
tested_on: 41-fn dev set, n=3 -- underpowered for this effect size

claim: The playbook levers appended by the verdict router (up to ~2200 chars) crowd large-function prompts and depress their scores.
source: hypothesis from the iter-4 mean regression
evidence: Tested by gating the playbook prose above 6000 chars of target asm (large block 2627 -> 446 chars). Large-tier mean recovered 21.6 -> 34.9, matching the prediction. BUT the small tier, whose prompts were byte-identical between the two runs (asm 1.5-3.1k, well under the gate), moved +9.8 on its own. An unchanged tier moving almost as much as the changed one means the recovery cannot be attributed to the gate. Exact went 12 -> 11. Kept -- it strictly reduces prompt size on large targets and cannot plausibly hurt -- but NOT confirmed. Note: this entry was already INCONCLUSIVE for the right reason -- the unchanged small tier moved almost as much as the gated large tier.

claim: Per-tier mean scores at n=10 are precise enough to attribute a change to an intervention.
evidence: The small tier received IDENTICAL prompts across iterations 4 and 5 and its mean moved +9.8 points (77.2 -> 87.0). So tier-mean run-to-run variance is roughly +/-10 at n=10, which is the same size as the effects being chased. Consequence: tier-mean deltas below ~10 points are not evidence. Either raise functions per tier, or run each configuration repeatedly and compare distributions. Whole-set exact counts are steadier but still swing by 1-2.
tested_on: iterations 4 and 5, small tier as an unintended control

claim: A permuter output directory named `output-100...` proves a byte-exact match.
source: own implementation, caught by external review
evidence: solver/pipeline.py::run_permuter parses a score from a DIRECTORY NAME and sets exact=True at >=100 without the oracle ever confirming it. This violates the project's foundational invariant -- byte-exact object comparison is the only source of truth. A false EXACT is worse than a missed match: it poisons every downstream number and the ratchet would lock it in. Every permuter result must be re-scored through workspace.score() and judged on 'Verified exact match'. SEVERITY WAS UNDERSTATED. Measured directly: permuter output directories are named by dist.py COST (lower is better), not by a percentage. output-3750 scores 17.98% through the oracle; output-3700 scores 21.83%; output-35 scores 99.36%. The old code read the directory number as a percentage and set exact=True at >=100, so nearly EVERY permuter output would have been declared a byte-exact match -- a 17.98% candidate included. It never fired only because no function in any completed run took the permute route. That is luck, not safety.

claim: Documenting a methodological risk in a module docstring is sufficient mitigation for it.
source: own practice, caught by external review
evidence: solver/siblings.py documents that a close twin carries real signal and that sibling runs must be reported separately -- and then every pipeline measurement ran with siblings enabled anyway, drawn from a 100%-complete repository the solver would not have mid-project. Writing the caveat did not change a single number. Mitigation means changing the experiment (git-history replay), not annotating it.

claim: Recording a new finding is enough; earlier conclusions it undermines will be noticed.
evidence: tier-means-underpowered-at-n10 (REFUTED) directly invalidates the CONFIRMED status of workbench-verdict-routing, and the two sat in the same bank unreconciled for two iterations. A finding that undermines prior conclusions must trigger a sweep of the entries it affects; nothing did that automatically.

claim: A patch script that prints 'patched' has applied its edit.
source: own practice, caught by a unit test
evidence: Three separate hint functions were written, unit-tested in isolation, and never wired in, because the composing edit's string replace silently did not match while the script printed 'patched' unconditionally. Two hypotheses were promoted to CONFIRMED on evidence that could not have come from them. A print statement is not a verification. Assert the OBSERVABLE EFFECT -- here, that hints_for_asm returns non-empty output for an asm containing the pattern -- not that the script ran.

claim: Supplying verified type facts (array stride, narrow parameter widths, frame size, KB access widths) will let the solver match medium and larger functions.
source: the premise behind six loop iterations of prompt enrichment
evidence: With the hints live for the first time, medium-tier mean went 49.8 -> 48.3 and exact stayed at 0. The routing shows why: ALL 10 medium and ALL 9 large functions routed to `reshape`, and not one reached `retype`, `permute` or `relocation`. Medium scores run 0-96%, mostly 27-55%. These are not near-misses with wrong types -- they are structurally wrong programs. Every type hint built targets the retype band, which medium functions do not reach, so the hints were aimed at a failure mode that is not occurring there. They did move `small` (79.5 -> 90.7, the only tier delta all night to clear the +/-10 noise floor), which is consistent: small functions DO sometimes reach retype.
tested_on: v3 dev run, 39/87 partial, paired against the pre-fix run

claim: The wall above `small` is structural -- wrong control flow and program shape -- not missing type information.
source: route distribution in the v3 run
evidence: CONFIRMED decisively, with zero GPU, by diagnosing objects already on disk from the v3 run. 30 of the 39 hard functions had usable candidates: 29 returned structure-mismatch (96.7%), 1 returned no verdict. Zero returned allocation, constant, frame-layout, schedule or relocation. By tier: medium 16/16, large 10/10, huge 3/3. Independently, 27 of 29 differ from the target in INSTRUCTION COUNT, which is structural by definition -- register allocation cannot change how many instructions exist. The earlier ambiguity is resolved: `reshape` was not merely the score<80 fallback, the workbench genuinely classifies these as structural. CONSEQUENCE: the wall is the model emitting a differently-shaped program, not missing facts about types. That explains every null result -- type hints, base resolution and the permuter all address non-structural residuals. The remaining levers are structural: sibling mirroring, decomposition, or model capability.
tested_on: 30 hard functions diagnosed from existing v3 objects

claim: Leaf functions are easier to match than non-leaf ones, so the eval set should stratify on it.
evidence: Measured over 68 completed functions: leaf 27.8% exact, non-leaf 28.1%. No difference whatsoever. Non-leaf functions actually have a HIGHER mean score (77.1 vs 62.2). Call count is not monotonic either -- functions with 1-4 calls match BEST (38.9%), better than functions with none. Inter-function context is not the difficulty. Half the eval stratification was spent on a non-factor.

claim: Match probability is governed by function size and memory-access density, with hard cliffs rather than a gradient.
source: predictor analysis of the v3 run
evidence: 68 functions. By instruction count: 71.4% / 15.0% / 5.9% / 0.0% across <20, 20-50, 50-120, 120+. By memory accesses: 66.7% / 28.0% / 0.0% / 0.0% across <5, 5-15, 15-40, 40+. TWO HARD CLIFFS: above 15 memory accesses, 0 of 25 matched; above 5 unknown-base accesses, 0 of 25 matched. These are not 'harder' regions, they are zero. Tier labels (tiny/small/medium/large) are just a proxy for instruction count.
tested_on: v3 dev run, 68 functions across 4 size tiers

claim: Improving the evidence tier's base resolution (currently 58.4%) would raise the match rate, because functions whose bases the KB cannot resolve are exactly the ones that fail.
evidence: REFUTED by the controlled test its own entry specified. Holding function size constant and splitting each band at its median unknown-base count: 0-20 insns low 62% vs high 88% (REVERSED), 20-50 low 20% vs high 11%, 50-120 low 9% vs high 0%, 120+ both 0%. The unknown/mem RATIO is non-monotonic across all sizes: 35%, 9%, 12%, 31%. The raw correlation was function size in disguise. CONSEQUENCE: improving the evidence tier's 58.4% base resolution would NOT raise the match rate, so dataflow analysis to resolve more bases is not the lever. Caveat: cells hold 4-13 functions, so this is suggestive rather than definitive -- but the reversal in the smallest band and the non-monotonic ratio both argue against a real effect. Mean scores do fall slightly with high unknown counts within bands; exact rate, which is what counts, does not.
tested_on: v3 run, 71 attempted functions, within-band split

claim: A function that errors during setup can be recorded at 0% alongside genuine model failures without distorting the result.
source: user asked whether an internet outage had corrupted the run
evidence: Two v3 functions were logged 0.00% with draws=0 and wall=0s -- no model call ever happened. They were request timeouts, recorded identically to functions the solver genuinely failed. Impact on the run: exact 27.5% -> 28.4%, mean 68.2% -> 70.2% once excluded. CAUSE: --timeout was lowered 900s -> 300s for v3 to bound a hung request, which converted two intermittently-slow calls into recorded failures; every earlier run used 900s and is clean. Ollama demonstrably stalls at times -- a 5-token prompt was measured at 76s. run_set now reports never-ran rows separately and excludes them from rates and means. Not caused by the network outage: the later of the two rows was written after connectivity returned.
tested_on: v3 dev run, 69 rows; audit of all 5 prior result files

claim: The correctness and routing work (hints wired in, verdict-first routing, oracle-verified permuting, adaptive context) raises the match rate.
source: an evening of fixes following external review
evidence: v3 dev run, 87 functions, first result with a config fingerprint. 84 attempted: 19 exact (22.6%), mean 60.9%. PAIRED against the pre-fix run on 65 shared functions: exact 19 -> 18, mean 69.75 -> 69.49. Both deltas sit well inside the measured noise floor (exact <3, mean <10), so the honest reading is NO CHANGE. By tier: tiny 71.4%, small 15.8%, medium 5.3%, large 0/15, huge 0/10 (first ever attempted, mean 9.6%). One match in 44 functions above `small`. The fixes remain correct and worth keeping -- run_permuter could fabricate an EXACT from a directory name, and the ratchet would have locked it in -- but correctness is not measured in score. They make the number trustworthy, not higher.
tested_on: v3 dev, 87 functions, fingerprinted, paired on 65

claim: A candidate scoring >=95% has a register-allocation residual, so the permuter can close it.
evidence: All three >=95% functions in the hard subset were routed to `reshape`, not `permute` -- and that is informative, because with an empty verdict the >=95% band falls back to permute. Getting reshape proves the workbench returned a STRUCTURAL verdict despite the high score. Tested directly on isRacePlayerRespawnSurfaceValid (95.77%): 400s of permuting produced 19 candidates, best oracle-verified 99.36%, no match. Prediction stated before the run and held. A high score does not imply the residual is allocation, which is exactly why routing on score alone was wrong.
tested_on: 3 near-misses routed; 1 permuted for 400s, 19 candidates verified

claim: A substantial share of large/huge-function generations are refusals recorded as failures, so those tiers' numbers are contaminated.
source: inspecting why huge-tier candidates were 5-instruction stubs
evidence: 96 of 694 candidate files (13.8%) contain refusal text. By tier: tiny 0/98 candidates, small 0/135, medium 11/123 (9%), large 47/96 (49%), huge 30/60 (50%). 87% of large functions and 80% of huge ones had at least one refused generation. The refusal rate tracks the performance collapse exactly. Best-of-3 with a 50% refusal rate is effectively best-of-1.5, so the large (0/15) and huge (0/10) results measure a model that declined half the attempts. Refusals also emit ~5-instruction stubs, which diagnose as structure-mismatch -- partially contaminating that finding for large/huge, though medium (9% refusals) stands. CORRECTION, from a follow-up check of my own claim: saying these tiers 'measure a model that declined half the attempts' OVERSTATED the contamination. best_score is a MAX across candidates and a refusal scores ~0, so a max ignores refusals. Measured directly: ZERO functions had no usable candidate -- every one got at least one genuine attempt, so the recorded scores stand. The real effect is UNDER-SAMPLING: usable draws were 100% for tiny/small, 91% medium, 52% large, 47% huge. Large and huge got about half the effective best-of-N. That does not rescue their results: tiny reaches 71% on ~4.7 usable draws while large gets 0% on ~3.3, and a 2x sampling deficit cannot produce a 71-point gap. Size remains the dominant factor; the refusals make those tiers under-sampled, not fabricated.
tested_on: 694 candidate files across the v3 run

claim: The refusals are triggered by 'You are decompiling a Nintendo 64 game' and will stop if the task is reframed as compiler-output reconstruction.
source: the obvious reading of the refusal text
evidence: Reframed the prompt to drop all game/decompilation framing and retested on two previously-refusing functions. The model still refused, adapting its wording to the new framing ('I can't provide the solution to this challenge', 'I can't produce the requested source'), and one variant wrote prose claiming the function was 'not recoverable from the given assembly dump'. Prediction was stated before the test and FAILED. This is capability capitulation wearing refusal language, not a safety refusal. Consequence: a prompt fix cannot recover the large/huge tiers; it needs a model that does not bail, or a task decomposed small enough that it does not want to.
tested_on: 2 previously-refusing functions, reframed prompt, n=2 each

claim: gpt-oss:20b's refusals on large/huge functions are costing matches; a model that attempts them would do better.
source: the natural reading of the refusal finding
evidence: Tested directly on three functions gpt-oss refused: ran qwen2.5-coder:14b, which produced NINE genuine attempts and zero refusals, up to 20KB of C per attempt. Scores: 0.00%, 0.87%, 0.00%. Attempting is worth no more than declining on these functions. Prediction stated beforehand -- qwen refuses less but scores no better -- and BOTH halves held. CONSEQUENCE: the refusals were a symptom, not a cause. Removing them recovers nothing, so the large/huge tiers are genuinely beyond both local models: one declines, the other emits confidently wrong code, and the outcome is identical.

claim: Splitting the READING of a long function across fresh instances, each seeing a bounded region, eliminates the refusals that appear only on long functions.
source: user's proposal: shifts and breaks, do not topple one instance
evidence: REPLICATED on 3 functions: drawMenuAsciiFontTile (182 lines, 4 regions), getRacePlayerRankingProgress (345, 8), checkMainMenuSecretCode (265, 6). 18 of 18 region reads succeeded, ZERO refusals -- against a baseline where these same functions refuse ~50% of the time when read whole (and where the composer, given the whole thing, refused 5 of 6 draws in the same run). Same model, same day, same flags: the only variable is how much it is asked to hold. This is now the only surviving explanation for the refusals -- copyright framing and capability capitulation are both REFUTED. SCOPE: this confirms bounded-region READING does not refuse. It does NOT claim regions produce matches; see the composer results, which are separate and much weaker. FURTHER REPLICATION (2026-08-28, entry 0): 27 more region reads across 6 functions, again ZERO refusals -- 45 of 45 region reads across 9 functions now. In the same run the composers, given those same functions whole, refused 9 of 36 draws. The region finding is unaffected by the compression result being killed: they are separate claims, and only the second failed. REPORTING CORRECTION (external review): excluding refusals from failure statistics is correct when measuring MODEL CAPABILITY, but wrong when measuring END-TO-END SYSTEM SUCCESS -- for an automated decompiler, a refusal is a failed attempt regardless of why. Both denominators must be reported side by side from now on. Past numbers quoting only the capability denominator flatter the system. FINAL SCOPE (2026-08-28): bounded reading eliminates refusals completely and reliably -- 45/45 region reads, 0/54 slices. But entry 2 showed that eliminating every refusal produces zero additional matches. The finding is real and narrow: it changes model BEHAVIOUR, not matching ability. It should not be cited as progress toward byte-exact reconstruction.

claim: A composer can write byte-exact C from region SUMMARIES alone, without the full assembly.
source: the obvious way to unload the composition step
evidence: Tested directly as arm B (summaries + lexicon, NO assembly) against arm C (summaries + lexicon + stripped assembly), same shared summaries, 6 draws each. B and C compiled equally often (2 of 6), but scored 0.8 vs 20.0 summed-best. Removing the assembly did not stop the composer refusing (3 of 6 either way) and cost nearly all of the score. So the detail cannot simply be dropped: a summary-only composer produces code that compiles and is wrong. The lexicon is a SUPPLEMENT to the assembly, not a replacement for it. Composition must stay grounded in the instructions.

claim: Stripping the /* offset vram encoding */ comments and attaching a lexicon of exact facts cuts the composer's input to ~34% and lets it attempt functions it otherwise refuses.
source: user's proposal: compress, plus a lexicon to check against, so it is lookup and not entire retrieval
evidence: KILLED by its own pre-registered kill condition at n=18 per arm (6 functions x 3 draws, stratified medium/large/huge). Refusals: A raw 4/18 (22%), C lexicon+stripped 5/18 (28%). The gap is -1 -- compression refused MORE. The condition was 'gap <= 1 means dead', and it is dead. Scores over compiled candidates: A mean 38.9 / median 29.7 (n=4), C mean 20.5 / median 17.7 (n=6). C compiled slightly more often (6 vs 4) but scored lower. Every one of those differences is below the significance floor, so the honest summary is NO EFFECT, with weak evidence of harm. The n=6 result that motivated this was noise, as flagged when it was recorded: arm A's 5/6 refusal rate there is 4/18 here. This is exactly why entry 0 existed and why nothing was built on it. CONSEQUENCE: strip_asm and lexicon() stay in the tree -- they are correct, validated at 82/82 globals, and lossless -- but they do NOT become the default composer path. A hypothesis does not get to change behaviour. NOTE the one striking datum, from the RAW arm: checkMainMenuSecretCode draw 1 scored 90.8%, the highest score this project has produced. Worth chasing on its own; it is not evidence for either arm. CAVEAT: two arm-A draws on drawPulsingAssetTableSprite returned in 0s and were counted 'no compile'. A 0s generation is almost certainly a degenerate empty response, so arm A's no-compile count is if anything flattered -- which does not change the verdict, since arm A already won.
tested_on: 6 functions x 3 draws x 2 arms, n=18 per arm (2026-08-28)

claim: Slices should emit C and carry forward the declarations made by earlier slices (WaDec 'temporal context'), instead of emitting prose summaries that one composer reads in a single shot.
evidence: Built and tested on 6 functions x 2 draws, paired against entry 0 arm A on the SAME functions. Clean run: 0 of 54 slices refused, 0 truncated, 1 of 54 empty. THE MECHANISM WORKS. Refusals went 4/18 (22%) to 0/12 (0%), at both slice and final level. Compile rate 22% -> 42%. That half of the prediction held. IT DOES NOT PRODUCE MATCHES, WHICH WAS THE POINT. Exact: 0, same as baseline. Mean score 39.0 -> 21.0, median 29.7 -> 18.1 -- both WORSE. The compile-rate gain (5/12 vs 4/18) is not significant at this n and is bought with markedly worse scores. AND IT IS ~17x MORE EXPENSIVE PER DRAW. Entry 0 produced 54 draws in 622s (~11.5s/draw including region summaries); entry 2 produced 12 draws in 2374s (~198s/draw). At equal compute the one-shot composer gets roughly 200 draws where sequential gets 12. Comparing at equal DRAW COUNT, as the harness did, flatters sequential composition enormously; at equal budget it loses decisively. This is the fair-comparison point an external review made, and it is what settles the entry. THE REAL FINDING, and it is the valuable one: we eliminated 100% of refusals and gained ZERO matches. That independently re-confirms [[refusals-are-a-symptom-not-a-cause]] from a different direction -- the refusal work was mechanically successful and NOT on the critical path. The stated risk came true as stated: register allocation is global and prefix-exact depth is 0, so C emitted a slice at a time does not compose into a byte-exact whole. Recording that as a real finding rather than explaining it away, as the entry required.

claim: Cut slices so that no loop body is split across a region boundary. (Marker substitution for nested loops was dropped -- see evidence.)
evidence: PREVALENCE FIRST, per the project rule. Over the 39 hard functions: 556 branch instructions, 17 backward branches, and the old branch-only rule split 7 of them (41% of loops) across a region boundary -- leaving a region holding a loop body whose head it cannot see. WaDec's concern is real here, not imported. IMPLEMENTED and verified mechanically: split loops 7 -> 0, and the change is confined to exactly the 4 functions that had split loops (35 of 39 produce byte-identical region boundaries). 32 unit tests pass. SCOPE, stated honestly: this is a CORRECTNESS fix, not a measured improvement. It touches 4 of 39 functions (10%), which is far too few to move any aggregate past the significance floor, so no score claim is made and none should be inferred. Its value is as a PREREQUISITE for [[sequential-slice-composition]]: a split loop costs little while regions only emit prose, but is fatal once regions emit C, because you cannot write half a loop. Measure it there, not here. DROPPED from the WaDec design: marker substitution for nested loops. Merging overlapping spans collapses nested loops into the outermost span, which already prevents every split; markers would add reassembly machinery for zero additional coverage at this prevalence. BUG CAUGHT, worth keeping as an instance of the standing pattern: the first version of the prevalence script reported 0 backward branches across 39 functions. That is impossible, and it was a parser bug -- split_regions preserves the /* offset vram encoding */ prefix, so a '^\s*b\w*' branch pattern never matched. A suspiciously clean zero is a broken measurement until proven otherwise; the script now asserts a non-zero branch count before drawing any conclusion.

claim: The lexicon should carry callee signatures, not just call sites.
evidence: Cheap and mechanical -- signatures are already in the KB. WaDec needs them for Wasm stack balance; for us a wrong argument count changes the call sequence and the frame.

claim: Moving the lexicon to the END of the prompt, adjacent to the instruction, beats its current position ahead of the assembly.
source: lost-in-the-middle (Liu et al., TACL 2024); Chroma Context Rot
evidence: Accuracy is a U-shape in position: start and end are attended, the middle drops over 30%. Our lexicon currently sits between the summaries and the assembly -- the worst position available. Nearly free to test: a string reorder, no new computation.

claim: Off-the-shelf prompt compression (LLMLingua) can shrink the composer's input.
evidence: Refuted on inspection rather than experiment, and the reason is categorical: LLMLingua is token-level and LOSSY by construction -- it drops tokens a small model judges redundant. Under a byte-exact criterion a dropped immediate is a wrong constant. strip_asm is the admissible kind of compression: lossless structural removal of fields (file offset, vram address, encoding) that provably cannot constrain the C source. Recorded so it is not retried as an obvious win.

claim: MEASURED: bounded-region prompts refuse far less than whole-function prompts on the same functions. INTERPRETATION (not established): the mechanism is abstention under uncertainty caused by context overload.
source: Chroma 'Context Rot' (18 models); our own region-split result
evidence: DOWNGRADED from CONFIRMED after external review, and the review is right. What is measured is solid and unchanged: 45 of 45 bounded region reads did not refuse, 0 of 54 slices refused, while the same functions read whole refuse ~22-50%. That is a real behavioural difference and it replicates. What is NOT established is the MECHANISM. Citing Chroma's Context Rot as support was overreach: Chroma observed 69 refusals in 194,480 calls, a completely different regime from a ~50% refusal rate, and it studied controlled retrieval and reasoning tasks rather than assembly translation. General long-context degradation is well evidenced; that it is the cause of THESE refusals is inference, not evidence. Two rival explanations remain untested: prompt-length-independent task difficulty (long functions are simply harder, and the model declines hard tasks), and format/complexity effects unrelated to length. Isolating the mechanism needs an experiment that varies length while holding difficulty fixed -- e.g. padding a SHORT function's prompt to the length of a long one and checking whether refusals appear. This entry was CONFIRMED on the strength of an interpretation, which is the exact evidence/inference boundary this project exists to police. Recorded as a process failure as much as a factual one.

claim: What predicts matching is the density of NAMED anchors (%hi/%lo globals and jal callees) per instruction, not function length.
source: cliff analysis of solved vs failing tiers
evidence: Formed on four groups where it looked decisive: solved small 0.210, failing medium 0.073, solved huge 0.170, failing huge 0.030 -- and it explained the anomaly that huge (40%) beats medium (10%), which length decay cannot. THEN TESTED ON TIERS NOT USED TO FORM IT, and it failed. Tiny solved came in high at 0.167 as predicted, but LARGE FAILING came in at 0.156 -- as anchor-dense as the solved groups, with 11 of 15 above the 0.10 threshold. Pooled: solved median 0.187 vs failing 0.096; 85% of solved vs 49% of failing above 0.10. A real correlation with heavy overlap, so a weak correlate and NOT a discriminator. Reporting the medians alone would have shipped a clean and wrong story. Kept as a cautionary entry: the hypothesis was generated and would have been confirmed on the same data. The out-of-sample check is the only reason it was caught.
tested_on: 87 v3 dev functions, out-of-sample on tiny/large (2026-08-28)

claim: The small->medium transition is a categorical cliff, not exponential decay in length; p^N is the wrong model.
source: per-tier match rates on v3 dev
evidence: Measured match rates: tiny 21/21 (100%), small 20/20 (100%), medium 2/20 (10%), large 1/16 (6%), huge 4/10 (40%). Two facts kill the p^N story that has driven weeks of work. First, 100% -> 10% between adjacent tiers is a cliff, not a smooth exponential. Second, HUGE (40%) BEATS MEDIUM (10%) -- under monotonic per-instruction decay the longest functions must be worst, and they are not. Consequence: small is fully solved and has no headroom left, so 'go back to smalls' is already satisfied. The frontier is MEDIUM. Consequence: length-management work (region splitting, compression, sequential composition) was aimed at a mechanism the tier data says is not the binding one -- consistent with entry 2, where removing 100% of refusals produced 0 matches. The solved-huge group looks like a distinct class: median 691 instructions with 54.5 calls, i.e. long stereotyped call sequences rather than dense algorithmic code.
